Bank of America estimates that an instantaneous 100 basis point parallel drop in rates would reduce its banking book net interest income by about $2.2 billion over 12 months, based on the June 30, 2026 10-Q. At December 31, 2025 the 10-K estimate was a $2.0 billion reduction, and at December 31, 2024 it was $2.3 billion. Management says the bank remains asset sensitive, so lower rates reduce net interest income.
In its most recent update (Q2 2026 10-Q, Table 41), Bank of America estimated that an instantaneous -100 bps parallel shift would change 12-month pretax net interest income by $(2.2) billion at June 30, 2026, a decline of about $2.2 billion. The comparable figure at December 31, 2025 was $(2.0) billion.
In the FY2025 10-K (Table 45), the estimated banking book net interest income change for a -100 bps instantaneous shift was $(2.0) billion at December 31, 2025, versus $(2.3) billion at December 31, 2024. The amounts reflect dynamic deposit sensitivities.
Bank of America states that it continues to be asset sensitive to a parallel move in interest rates, with most of that impact coming from the short end of the yield curve. This is why falling rates reduce net interest income.
The sensitivity analysis assumes that Bank of America takes no action in response to the rate shocks. In lower-rate scenarios it also assumes that a portion of higher-yielding deposits or market-based funding is replaced with low-cost or noninterest-bearing deposits. It does not assume changes in other macroeconomic variables normally correlated with rate changes.
Management notes that larger or deeper declines can behave non-linearly. If long-end rates fell significantly, for example over 200 bps, customer prepayments would generally increase, with an incremental reduction to net interest income. Where rates are already low, the ability to further reduce rates paid on deposits is reduced as customer rates near zero.
